q: Photosynthesis is the chemical reaction that occurs when plants use energy from the sun, carbon dioxide, and water to synthesise the food that the plant needs to survive.
e: True. Photosynthesis is the chemical reaction that occurs when plants use energy from the sun, carbon dioxide, and water to synthesise the food that the plant needs to survive. Oxygen is a product of that reaction, not a starting material.

q: Photosynthesis is the chemical reaction that occurs when plants use energy from the sun, carbon dioxide, and oxygen to synthesise the food that the plant needs to survive.
e: False. Plants use carbon dioxide and water, not oxygen, as the starting materials. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis.

q: Except for the energy produced from nuclear reactors, all of man's energy resources are chemicals or involve the utilisation of energy through chemical reactions.
e: True. Except for the energy produced from nuclear reactors, all of man's energy resources are chemicals or involve the utilisation of energy through chemical reactions. Fossil fuels, food, and batteries all store or release chemical energy.

q: Except for the energy produced from solar cells, all of man's energy resources are chemicals or involve the utilisation of energy through chemical reactions.
e: False. The exception named in this lesson is nuclear reactors. Solar cells are not that nuclear exception.

q: Whenever a chemical reaction occurs, energy is usually transferred to or from the surroundings.
e: True. Whenever a chemical reaction occurs, energy is usually transferred to or from the surroundings. That transfer is why flasks feel hot or cold.

q: Changing states of matter also involve energy changes.
e: True. Changing states of matter also involve energy changes. Melting and boiling take energy in; freezing and condensing give energy out, with no new substance.

q: Evaporation, melting, condensation, and sublimation are some examples of chemical changes around us in everyday life.
e: False. Those are changes of state, so they are physical changes. No new substance is made.

q: A process that can take place on its own accord is called spontaneous.
e: True. A process that can take place on its own accord is called spontaneous. Spontaneous does not always mean fast; rusting is spontaneous and slow.

q: A process that can take place on its own accord is called non-spontaneous.
e: False. A process that runs on its own is spontaneous. Non-spontaneous changes need a continuous energy push.

q: Non-spontaneous processes need the energy to take place.
e: True. Non-spontaneous processes need the energy to take place. Without a continuous energy supply they do not keep going.

q: Almost all chemical reactions absorb or release energy, generally in the form of heat.
e: True. Almost all chemical reactions absorb or release energy, generally in the form of heat. Chemists track that heat as the enthalpy change.

q: Adding a solution of dilute sulphuric acid to a solution of sodium hydroxide is an example of a spontaneous reaction.
e: True. Adding a solution of dilute sulphuric acid to a solution of sodium hydroxide is an example of a spontaneous reaction. Acid-base neutralisation runs on its own and gives out heat.

q: Adding a solution of dilute sulphuric acid to a solution of sodium hydroxide is an example of a non-spontaneous reaction.
e: False. Acid-base neutralisation of this kind runs on its own, so it is spontaneous. You do not have to keep feeding energy in.

q: The reaction between magnesium and oxygen, and the reaction between copper and oxygen are both non-spontaneous reactions.
e: True. The reaction between magnesium and oxygen, and the reaction between copper and oxygen are both non-spontaneous reactions. Copper needs heating in air; it does not keep reacting on its own at room temperature the way sodium would.

q: Iron rusting is endothermic and spontaneous.
e: False. Rusting is spontaneous, but it is exothermic. The iron-oxygen reaction releases heat overall.

q: When the ice melts at room temperature, that is a spontaneous and endothermic process.
e: True. When the ice melts at room temperature, that is a spontaneous and endothermic process. The ice takes heat from the room, so the process is endothermic even though it happens by itself.

q: When sulphuric acid is slowly poured into water, the flask or beaker becomes hot.
e: True. When sulphuric acid is slowly poured into water, the flask or beaker becomes hot. That heat release means the mixing is exothermic.

q: Exothermic reactions give out energy, so there is a temperature fall.
e: False. If the reaction gives out energy, the surroundings get warmer. A temperature fall would mean heat is being taken in.

q: In exothermic reactions, the energy of the product is lower than the energy of the reactants because energy has been released during the reaction.
e: True. In exothermic reactions, the energy of the product is lower than the energy of the reactants because energy has been released during the reaction. That drop in enthalpy is the definition of an exothermic reaction.

q: When ammonium chloride is dissolved in water, the flask becomes quite cold to the touch.
e: True. When ammonium chloride is dissolved in water, the flask becomes quite cold to the touch. The dissolving takes heat in, so it is endothermic.

q: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so there is a temperature rise.
e: False. Taking heat in cools the surroundings, so the thermometer falls. A temperature rise belongs to an exothermic change.

q: In endothermic reactions, the energy of the products is higher than the energy of the reactants because energy has been absorbed during the reaction.
e: True. In endothermic reactions, the energy of the products is higher than the energy of the reactants because energy has been absorbed during the reaction. That rise in enthalpy is an endothermic reaction.

q: Energy changes in chemical reactions are caused by the making and breaking of chemical bonds.
e: True. Energy changes in chemical reactions are caused by the making and breaking of chemical bonds. Breaking absorbs energy; making releases energy.

q: Energy is released to break bonds, so bond breaking is an exothermic process.
e: False. You must put energy in to break bonds. Bond breaking is endothermic; bond making is the step that releases energy.

q: Energy is released when new bonds form, so bond making is an exothermic process.
e: True. Energy is released when new bonds form, so bond making is an exothermic process. The opposite step, breaking a bond, is endothermic.

q: If the energy absorbed in bond breaking is more than the energy given out in bond making, the reaction is exothermic.
e: False. If bond breaking costs more than bond making returns, the system has absorbed heat overall. That reaction is endothermic.

q: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
e: True. The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed. Energy is never created or destroyed in a chemical change; it only changes form or moves between system and surroundings.

q: Energy can change from one form to another without a net loss or gain of energy and it is called energy transformation.
e: True. Energy can change from one form to another without a net loss or gain of energy and it is called energy transformation. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The specific part of the universe that contains the reaction or process which is studied is called the surroundings.
e: False. That chosen piece is the system. The surroundings are everything else.

q: Everything in the universe other than the system is called the surroundings.
e: True. Everything in the universe other than the system is called the surroundings. The system is the reaction you are watching; the surroundings are everything else.

q: The total chemical energy of a substance is called its enthalpy.
e: True. The total chemical energy of a substance is called its enthalpy. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: The change in enthalpy describes the amount of heat transferred at constant volume during a chemical reaction.
e: False. Enthalpy change is the heat transferred at constant pressure. Constant-volume heat is a different quantity, q_v.

q: The unit of enthalpy change is kilojoule per mole ($kJ mol^{-1}$).
e: True. The unit of enthalpy change is kilojoule per mole (kJmol-1). Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: The change in enthalpy is expressed as $\Delta H = H_{reactants} - H_{products}$.
e: False. Delta H is H(products) minus H(reactants). Swapping that order flips the sign.

q: For an endothermic reaction where energy is absorbed from the surroundings, the total energy of the products is greater than that of the reactants, then $\Delta H$ is positive.
e: True. For an endothermic reaction where energy is absorbed from the surroundings, the total energy of the products is greater than that of the reactants, then deltaH is positive. Endothermic means the system takes in heat, so delta H is positive.

q: For an exothermic reaction where energy is released to the surroundings, the total energy of the products is less than that of the reactants, then $\Delta H$ is negative.
e: True. For an exothermic reaction where energy is released to the surroundings, the total energy of the products is less than that of the reactants, then deltaH is negative. Exothermic means the system releases heat, so delta H is negative.

q: The standard conditions chosen for energy changes are standard temperature $0^\circ C$ and standard pressure $1 atm$.
e: False. Thermochemical standard temperature is 25 degrees Celsius, 298 K, not 0 degrees. Pressure is 1 atm, or 1 bar in later books.

q: A thermochemical equation is a balanced chemical equation that includes the physical states of all reactants and products and the standard enthalpy change.
e: True. A thermochemical equation is a balanced chemical equation that includes the physical states of all reactants and products and the standard enthalpy change. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: The standard enthalpy change of formation of a compound is the enthalpy change when two moles of a compound are formed from its elements under standard conditions.
e: False. Standard enthalpy of formation is for one mole of compound from its elements in standard states. Two moles would double the value.

q: The state symbol for carbon is shown as graphite because it is the most stable form of carbon.
e: True. The state symbol for carbon is shown as graphite because it is the most stable form of carbon. pH is the negative log of [H+], so a smaller pH means a more acidic solution.

q: The standard enthalpy change of combustion is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burnt completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
e: True. The standard enthalpy change of combustion is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burnt completely in oxygen under standard conditions. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: Combustion reactions are always endothermic and the enthalpy changes are always positive.
e: False. Combustion releases heat, so it is exothermic and delta H is negative. Fuels burn because the products are lower in enthalpy.

q: The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when solutions of an acid and an alkali react together under standard conditions to produce one mole of water.
e: True. The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when solutions of an acid and an alkali react together under standard conditions to produce one mole of water. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: The neutralisation reaction is endothermic and the enthalpy change is positive.
e: False. Neutralisation of a strong acid with a strong base is exothermic. Heat is given out and delta H is negative.

q: Experimentally, $\Delta H$ is not measured directly; the heat change, $q$, is measured.
e: True. Experimentally, deltaH is not measured directly; the heat change, q, is measured. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The heat change is calculated using the equation $q = m \Delta T / c$.
e: False. The calorimetry equation is q = m c delta T. You multiply by specific heat capacity; you do not divide by it.

q: A calorimeter is a device to measure the amount of heat released or absorbed in reactions that occur in solutions.
e: True. A calorimeter is a device to measure the amount of heat released or absorbed in reactions that occur in solutions. A calorimeter measures heat by tracking the temperature change of a known mass of water or solution.

q: The amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one gram of water by one degree is known as the specific heat capacity of water.
e: True. The amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one gram of water by one degree is known as the specific heat capacity of water. Higher temperature means a larger fraction of particles have energy at least Ea.

q: If $\Delta T$ is a positive value, the $q$ value will also be positive, but the actual sign on $\Delta H$ is negative because the reaction is giving off this amount of energy.
e: True. If deltaT is a positive value, the q value will also be positive, but the actual sign on deltaH is negative because the reaction is giving off this amount of energy. The because-clause is the chemical reason that makes the statement hold.

q: A bomb calorimeter is a type of calorimeter for determining the heat of combustion by igniting a sample in a high pressure of oxygen in a sealed vessel.
e: True. A bomb calorimeter is a type of calorimeter for determining the heat of combustion by igniting a sample in a high pressure of oxygen in a sealed vessel. A calorimeter measures heat by tracking the temperature change of a known mass of water or solution.

q: The highly accurate values of the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation can be measured only by a bomb calorimeter.
e: False. Neutralisation is done in solution, so a simple coffee-cup or solution calorimeter is the usual tool. A bomb calorimeter is for combustion.

q: Enthalpy change is the heat change accompanying a chemical reaction at constant pressure.
e: True. Enthalpy change is the heat change accompanying a chemical reaction at constant pressure. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: Because the solution is very dilute, its specific heat capacity is taken to be the same as that of water.
e: True. Because the solution is very dilute, its specific heat capacity is taken to be the same as that of water. Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 degree Celsius.

q: The enthalpy change of solution, $\Delta H_{sol}$, of a substance, is the enthalpy change when two moles of the substance are dissolved in water.
e: False. Enthalpy of solution is defined per one mole dissolved to infinite dilution, or to a stated concentration. Two moles is the wrong amount.

q: There are very few reactions whose enthalpy change can be measured directly by measuring the change in temperature in a calorimeter.
e: True. There are very few reactions whose enthalpy change can be measured directly by measuring the change in temperature in a calorimeter. Higher temperature means a larger fraction of particles have energy at least Ea.

q: By using Hess's law, the enthalpy change for reactions that are difficult to carry out individually can be determined indirectly.
e: True. By using Hess's law, the enthalpy change for reactions that are difficult to carry out individually can be determined indirectly. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is different, depending on the route taken from reactants to products.
e: False. Hess's law says delta H depends only on the start and finish. The path you take does not change the overall enthalpy.

q: Hess's law can be illustrated by drawing an enthalpy cycle.
e: True. Hess's law can be illustrated by drawing an enthalpy cycle. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: The standard enthalpy change for the formation of an element in its standard state is one.
e: False. Formation enthalpy of an element in its standard state is zero, not one. That is the baseline for all other formation values.

q: To determine the enthalpy change of reaction from enthalpy changes of formation, the corresponding elements of reactant and product should be considered.
e: True. To determine the enthalpy change of reaction from enthalpy changes of formation, the corresponding elements of reactant and product should be considered. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: To determine the enthalpy change of formation from enthalpy changes of combustion, the corresponding combustion products should be considered.
e: True. To determine the enthalpy change of formation from enthalpy changes of combustion, the corresponding combustion products should be considered. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: Enthalpy changes are due to the breaking and forming of bonds.
e: True. Enthalpy changes are due to the breaking and forming of bonds. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: Breaking a bond releases energy and making a bond absorbs energy.
e: False. Breaking a bond absorbs energy and making a bond releases energy. The stem has those two directions swapped.

q: The energy needed to make or break bonds is called bond energy or bond enthalpy.
e: True. The energy needed to make or break bonds is called bond energy or bond enthalpy. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: The higher the bond enthalpy, the less energy needed to break the bond, and the weaker is the bond.
e: False. A higher bond enthalpy means more energy is needed to break the bond, so the bond is stronger. Weak bonds have small bond enthalpies.

q: The symbol for bond enthalpy is $E$.
e: True. The symbol for bond enthalpy is E. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: When new bonds are formed the amount of energy released is greater than the amount of energy absorbed when the same type of bond is broken.
e: False. Breaking and making the same bond cost and return the same energy. You cannot gain energy by forming the identical bond you just broke.

q: Hess's law can also be used to find approximate values of enthalpy change of a reaction using bond enthalpies.
e: True. Hess's law can also be used to find approximate values of enthalpy change of a reaction using bond enthalpies. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: In burning fuels such as paraffin, coal, propane, and butane, the exothermic reaction takes place during the reaction.
e: True. In burning fuels such as paraffin, coal, propane, and butane, the exothermic reaction takes place during the reaction. Exothermic means the system releases heat, so delta H is negative.

q: The exothermic reaction takes place during cooking food, baking bread, boiling water and warming the food.
e: False. Cooking, baking, and boiling take heat in from the stove, so those changes are endothermic for the food or water. The flame is exothermic, but the processes named in the stem are not.

q: Hand warmers produce heat from the exothermic reaction.
e: True. Hand warmers produce heat from the exothermic reaction. Exothermic means the system releases heat, so delta H is negative.

q: A lot of weight loss applications use the Law of Conservation of Mass concept to calculate the number of calories burned during a workout.
e: False. Calories are an energy count, so you use conservation of energy, not conservation of mass. Mass is not what those apps are adding up.

q: In an exothermic reaction, the surrounding temperature is increased.
e: True. In an exothermic reaction, the surrounding temperature is increased. Higher temperature means a larger fraction of particles have energy at least Ea.

q: Total enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is dependent on the route by which the reaction takes place.
e: False. Total enthalpy change is a state function, so it does not depend on the route. That is Hess's law.

q: Standard enthalpy change is measured at $25^\circ C$ and $760 mmHg$.
e: True. Standard enthalpy change is measured at 25degreesC and 760mmHg. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.

q: When the energy needed to break bonds is greater than the energy needed to form bonds, the reaction is exothermic.
e: False. If breaking costs more than forming returns, the reaction absorbs heat and is endothermic. Exothermic is the opposite balance.

q: A process in which the system absorbs heat from its surroundings is called an endothermic process.
e: True. A process in which the system absorbs heat from its surroundings is called an endothermic process. Endothermic means the system takes in heat, so delta H is positive.

q: Heat liberated by a chemical reaction is assigned a positive sign.
e: False. Heat given out is given a negative delta H. The system has lost energy, so the sign is minus.

q: Change in enthalpy of a system is due to the heat supplied at a constant pressure.
e: True. Change in enthalpy of a system is due to the heat supplied at a constant pressure. Enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released at constant pressure.
